page.text:
Group actions translate abstract algebraic structure into concrete
combinatorics and geometry.

A classic instance is the *conjugation action* of a group $G$ on itself:
$g \cdot x = g * x * g^{-1}$. In this setting:
- The orbit of $x$ is the *conjugacy class* $\operatorname{Cl}(x)$.
- The stabilizer of $x$ is the *centralizer*
  $C_G(x) = \{g \in G : g * x = x * g\}$.
- The fixed points of the action form the center $Z(G)$.

Applying the Orbit-Stabilizer theorem to this action yields the
celebrated *Class Equation* for a finite group:
$$ |G| = |Z(G)| + \sum_{i=1}^k [G : C_G(x_i)], $$ where $x_1, \dots, x_k$
are representatives of the non-central conjugacy classes. The Class
Equation is a cornerstone of finite group theory, proving for instance
that every non-trivial finite $p$-group has a non-trivial center, and
opening the gateway to the Sylow theorems.
